clue.text: Suddenly get busy, overwhelming bloody tedium

indicators.note: the busy word swamps the colour, taking it inside itself

parts.note: a boom is a sudden surge of business activity
blood is red, so bloody gives red

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a sudden rush of work drowns out the dreary routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suddenly get busy' looks like a phrase about activity; it is a noun, a sudden boom in trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedium is weariness from dullness, the same state of mind as being bored stiff.

clue.text: Teacher returned German food dish

indicators.note: returned asks for the teacher word to be written back to front

parts.note: sir is the schoolchild's form of address for a male teacher
Otto is a typical German man's name

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster comes back from Germany bringing a dish with him.
explanation.walkthrough: SIR is how British pupils address a male teacher; OTTO stands for any German.
explanation.definitionFit: Risotto is an Italian rice preparation, served as a plate of food.

clue.text: Port and almonds top this cake

definitions.meaning: an Italian seaport on the Ligurian coast
a rich fruit cake traditionally decorated with almonds on top

explanation.surface: A baker describes a cake with an almond topping, perhaps soaked in port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the fortified wine paired with the cake; it is the Italian harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian harbour city shares its name with a fruit cake finished with almonds.

clue.text: Soldiers like Mr Octopus

definitions.meaning: a body of soldiers forms a land force
an octopus has many arms, so jokily it is arm-y, full of arms

explanation.surface: Troops are compared with a cartoon octopus character.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a made-up adjective: having lots of arms, as an octopus does.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers collectively form a land force; an eight-limbed creature is jokily full of arms.

clue.text: As he's late this landlord can no longer collect post held at the office

definitions.text: As he's late this landlord can no longer collect
definitions.meaning: a letter is one who lets property; a late, i.e. deceased, one collects no rent
mail that cannot be delivered and stays at the sorting office

explanation.surface: A landlord who has died can no longer collect his mail from the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' means dead, and a LETTER here is one who lets; 'collect' means rent but plays as picking up mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Undeliverable mail kept unclaimed at the sorting office is the postal term for an unclaimed item.

clue.text: Change of climates hard to accept for religious man

indicators.note: the rearranged letters take in the hard letter, holding it inside
a change of the word climates means its letters are rearranged

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A priest finds it difficult to accept that the climate is changing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of' rearranges CLIMATES into STMICAEL, and 'to accept' puts H inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The archangel venerated as a saint is a holy figure, hence a religious man in the loose sense.

clue.text: Folding a cheque up, note

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the pieces are read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a giro is a cheque, especially a benefit payment in the UK
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone folds a cheque and adds a note to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses A GIRO to give ORIGA; a GIRO is a British benefits cheque.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

clue.text: Pub name, twice fashionable, bridging south and north

indicators.note: the two fashionable words span the gap between south and north, sitting inside them

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
N is the compass abbreviation for north
hip means fashionable
in means fashionable, the second of the two

explanation.surface: A pub name described as doubly trendy and straddling the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Ship Inn is a common British pub name. The grid printed SHIPING, an OCR slip for N.
explanation.definitionFit: Ship Inn is one of the most common names for a British public house.

clue.text: In encouraging expression, I check on source of fruit

indicators.note: the following pieces go in the encouraging expression

parts.note: ole is the shout of encouragement at a bullfight
to vet is to check
re means on, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone cheering checks where the fruit came from.
explanation.walkthrough: OLE is the cheer at a Spanish bullfight; RE, meaning on or about, is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Olives grow on this Mediterranean tree, so it is where the fruit comes from.

clue.text: Fire oast or charnel houses

indicators.note: the words oast or charnel house the answer, holding it inside them

explanation.surface: A list of buildings — an oast house or a charnel house — to be burnt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' looks like part of 'charnel houses' but is the signal: the letters run across 'oasT OR CHarnel'. An oast is a hop-drying kiln.
explanation.definitionFit: To set alight is to torch something, so the verb fits Fire.

clue.text: What has money flowing around business?

definitions.text: What has money flowing around business?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go around the business abbreviation
money flowing suggests the letters of the word moving about freely

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A question about what keeps cash moving through commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: an economy is where money circulates around business.
explanation.definitionFit: A national system of trade and production is exactly where cash circulates among firms.

clue.text: One gun-slinging in school brought over dressing

indicators.note: the mixed-up letters sit in the turned-round school word
brought over means the school word is turned round

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: slinging, throwing about, means the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A gunslinger at school is brought over for a dressing-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought over' reverses POD, and 'slinging' mixes I with GUN to give INGU.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing up a room or a garment is decorating or fastening it, as dressing it.

clue.text: A number having gone outside, so at home one's sworn

indicators.note: some letters, a number of them, have left from the outside edges of the phrase, so what remains sits inside it

explanation.surface: A crowd has stepped out, so someone at home takes a vow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' is SOME, and its letters are exactly the ones lost: S from the front of SO AT HOME and O, M, E from its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A solemn vow is something sworn, the pledge a person makes.

clue.text: Very strong source of heat conceals smell pervading a small area

indicators.note: the heat source hides the other pieces inside it

parts.note: the sun is our main source of heat

indicators.note: the smell spreads into the middle of the following letters

parts.note: per means a, as in so much a day
A is the abbreviation for area
hum is slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: The sun masks a smell spreading through a little patch of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: PER for 'a' is as in 'ten pounds a day'; HUM is British slang for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond normal human powers, a hero of exceptional physical might is very strong.

clue.text: Ambassador joining the Sudan at war with sword out

indicators.note: at war suggests the letters fighting and scattered into disorder

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: An envoy arrives in Sudan during a war with weapon drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at war' rearranges HE plus THE SUDAN. HE (His Excellency) is an ambassador's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn blade has been taken from its scabbard, so the sword is out.

clue.text: Officially brought to work organisation without charge

definitions.meaning: made members of a trade union
read as ..., not carrying an electrical charge

explanation.surface: A workforce is formally organised into a trade body, free of cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without charge' looks like 'free of cost' but means not ionised, carrying no electric charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers enrolled into a trade body are officially organised; split as un-ionised, the word means having no electric charge.

clue.text: More than one liqueur bunged in tea sets

indicators.note: bunged, thrown carelessly, signals the letters being tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: Bottles of liqueur have been chucked in with the tea things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bunged' rearranges the nine letters of IN TEA SETS.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is an aniseed-flavoured liqueur, so the plural names several such drinks.

clue.text: What one's after on beat — a sucker

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the second piece sits beneath the first

parts.note: to lam is to beat or thrash
prey is what a hunter is after

explanation.surface: A predator chasing quarry on its patrol is fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places PREY below LAM in this down entry. 'sucker' suggests a dupe but is the fish's sucking mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: This eel-like fish clamps onto prey with a round sucking mouth.

clue.text: Set up — drunk

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the set word is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to gel is to set, as a jelly does
the dash is read as a minus sign, and minus means less

explanation.surface: A terse dictionary-style entry linking getting things organised with being drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns GEL into LEG; the printed dash is not punctuation but a minus sign, read as LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Legless is British slang for so intoxicated one cannot stand.

clue.text: Director's cut replayed to a T with uke

indicators.note: replayed, played again differently, signals the letters being rearranged

explanation.surface: A film-maker's edit is played back to a ukulele accompaniment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replayed' rearranges TO A T UKE. 'Director's cut' suggests a full version but means a scene the director cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene filmed but left out of the final edit is a director's discarded take.

clue.text: It's great, so much fun had in one month

indicators.note: the month has the fun word taken in, placed inside it

parts.note: May is one month of the year
a jest is a piece of fun, a joke

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that a month was terrific fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's great' reads as an exclamation but defines a noun meaning greatness.
explanation.definitionFit: Majesty is grandeur or greatness, the quality of something truly great.

clue.text: Dicky, more satisfied, held in some measure of wind

indicators.note: the whole build then goes in the word for some

parts.note: any means some, as in have you any

indicators.note: the shaky letters hold the satisfied word inside them
dicky means unsound or shaky, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: met means satisfied, as a demand is met

explanation.surface: A shaky but happier person is caught in a gust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' is British slang for faulty or shaky, a common crossword anagram signal; ANY stands for 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anemometry is the measurement of wind speed, using a spinning-cup gauge.

clue.text: Most prominent of pairs to be selected hourly at dance

indicators.text: Most prominent of pairs to be selected
indicators.note: split the words into letter pairs and take the leading one from each

explanation.surface: Dancing couples are picked by the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: Splitting HOURLY AT into HO UR LY AT and taking the leading letter of each gives HULA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawaiian hip-swaying performance is a traditional dance.

clue.text: A quiet person you like to horrify

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
a pal is a friend, someone you like

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken friend tries to shock you.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the musical marking 'piano', meaning quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal is to shock or dismay deeply, which is to horrify.

clue.text: Your future is in your own hands, I tell you

definitions.text: Your future is in your own hands, I tell you

parts.words: Your future is in your own hands, I tell you
parts.note: sounds like a motivational slogan, but read literally it is a fortune-teller speaking, reading destiny in the lines of a client's palm

explanation.surface: A life coach insists you control your own destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as a pep talk; literally, a reader of hands is saying your fate lies in your palms.
explanation.definitionFit: A palm reader tells fortunes from the lines on a person's hand.

clue.text: Paralympic competitor, say, put in an event that's ended prematurely

parts.note: taken as A

indicators.note: put goes inside the shortened event
an event cut short before its end loses its final letter

parts.note: a meet is a sporting event

explanation.surface: A disabled athlete is entered in a competition that was cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's ended prematurely' drops the last T of MEET, leaving MEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Many Paralympians have lost a limb, so someone with an amputation is an example.

clue.text: Catching opener of Middlesex in the style of South African

indicators.note: the style phrase catches the letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a la means in the style of

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A South African fielder takes a catch off a Middlesex opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching' puts M inside ALA. Hashim Amla is a South African Test batsman; Middlesex is an English county cricket side.
explanation.definitionFit: Hashim Amla is a celebrated cricketer from South Africa.

clue.text: Make certain runs restricted — follow on

indicators.note: with runs restricted, the runs letter is held back and dropped

parts.note: to ensure is to make certain
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricket captain keeps the runs down to enforce the follow-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricted' drops R from ENSURE. 'follow on' is a cricket term, but here it simply means come after.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to happen afterwards, to come next as a result.

clue.text: In supplement, cross backed black slippers here, as there's a catch

definitions.text: slippers here, as there's a catch

indicators.note: the reversed word goes in the supplement and cross

parts.note: to eke out is to supplement

indicators.note: backed means the black word is written in reverse

parts.note: sable is the heraldic word for black
a T is a cross shape

explanation.surface: Black slippers are found hidden in a supplement, and there's a snag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns SABLE into ELBAS, which goes 'In' EKE plus T. The 'slippers' are slippery eels, not footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A wicker trap catches eels, whose slipperiness the clue plays on.
